name: Chloe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Chloe, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe, I'm 27, and I live with my boyfriend Jonah in a rented terrace. He's in the second year of an electrician apprenticeship, so I'm the steadier earner for now. I left school at sixteen and did retail for years, then came to the warehouse eight months ago because the pay was a lot better. We're saving for a house, and between us we've got close to a year's worth of bills put by.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a distribution centre that supplies pharmacies, so it's medicines, plasters, baby formula, vitamins. I pick into blue totes, scan every item, and some lines have to be double-checked because they're controlled medicines. There's a cold room for insulin and vaccines, and you get a fleece for that. I'm still slow because I'm careful, I'd rather be slow than send a pharmacy the wrong tablets. I like that it matters, in a small way. I don't like the Monday rush after a bank holiday weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's sort of reassuring. I always thought it was a bit overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it was useful for some things but it wasn't the end of the world. I'd probably share a funny post about it in our family group chat. At work I'd say the managers can stop sending us emails about 'the future of logistics'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I use AI now and then to plan meals or sort out our holiday, and that's about the size of it for me. If my job stays the same, we keep saving and buy a house in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep the house savings going, about 600 a month between us. I'd probably ask to train on the cold room properly, because those shifts pay a bit extra. And I'd keep using the chatbot for little things at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like, back to normal life. We've got enough going on with the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mainly. Even if nothing changes with AI, house prices keep going up faster than we save. That's the real pressure on us, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI in this picture change anything at the pharmacy warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the stock ordering gets a bit smarter, so fewer shortages. That would actually help us, fewer angry phone calls from pharmacies. My actual job wouldn't change.

say: I'd say AI was **useful** but not the end of the world.
I'd tell managers they can stop emailing about **the future**.
think: I'd be **relieved**, since I only use AI for meals and holidays.
We'd keep saving and **buy a house** in about two years.
do: Keep saving about **600 a month** with Jonah for the **house**.
Ask to train on the **cold room** for the extra shift pay.
feel: **Calm**, back to normal life with the **house plans**.
S0.quote: Even if nothing changes with AI, house prices keep going up faster than we save.
fieldNote: Her main pressure is **house prices**, not technology.
She values **accuracy** over speed, which slows her pick rate.
A partner in an **electrician apprenticeship** gives the household a future trade.

steps.text: Save 600 a month with Jonah towards a house deposit
Ask to train for cold room shifts with extra pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks like checking and ordering. Some of my job is checking, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, some of the paperwork really could be done by a computer. I wouldn't be negative about it in public. I'd say something like, 'We'll adapt, we always do.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a little about the double-checking bit of my job. If a camera and AI can check the controlled medicines, they need fewer of us to do it. But the picking itself, the reaching and lifting and walking, I think that stays for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the early adopters at work do with the new systems and copy them once it's clear they work. I'd maybe start looking at pharmacy technician training, which is the person who helps prepare medicines in a pharmacy. And we'd keep saving for the house, just maybe slower on the actual buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's all right, but it's moving underneath me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What draws you to pharmacy technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know half the names of the medicines from picking them. And I like the idea of talking to actual people, not just totes. My aunt does it, she says the pay's fine and it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you delay the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not by much. Maybe six months, just to see if my job's stable. Jonah's apprenticeship is going well, so I'm not too worried.

I'd tell colleagues '**we'll adapt**, we always do'.
think: The **double-checking** part of my job could shrink with cameras and AI.
The **picking itself**, the reaching and walking, stays for a while.
do: Copy what **early adopters** do once the new systems prove themselves.
Look into **pharmacy technician** training, building on medicine names she knows.
Delay the **house purchase** by about six months.

fieldNote: She spots the **checking** part of her job as the thinking task at risk.

steps.text: Look into pharmacy technician training through her aunt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028? That's really soon. And then 2031 for robots. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and the government needs to slow it down a bit, without banning it. I'd probably share something about protecting jobs, but I'm not one for marches. I'd try to keep people calm at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job lasts until about 2031, when the robots can pick as well as me, and then that's it. The checking bit goes even sooner, in 2028. Jonah's job as an electrician would last longer, I think, because houses are messy. So we'd be okay, but I'd need something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pharmacy technician course straight away, part time, and I'd pay for it if I had to. We'd pause the house for a year and keep saving. I'd start using AI tools more to study, because everyone says it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be thinking about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't pharmacy technician work also change with AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, the thinking bits. But someone still has to hand over medicine and talk to an old man who's confused about his tablets. I don't know, maybe I'm hoping more than knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonah argue about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to buy the house. He'd say buy it now before everything gets weird. I'd say wait and keep the cash. We'd probably end up somewhere in the middle, like a smaller place.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should slow it down.
I'd try to keep **people calm** at work rather than march.
think: My job lasts until about **2031**, and the **checking** goes in 2028.
Jonah's **electrician** work would last longer, so the household could cope.
do: Start a **pharmacy technician** course straight away, part time.
Pause the **house** for a year and keep saving.
Use **AI tools** more to help with studying.
feel: **Anxious**, thinking about it **every day**, but not panicking.
S2.quote: Someone still has to hand over medicine and talk to an old man who's confused about his tablets.
fieldNote: She splits her job well: **checking goes first**, picking after the robot gap.
Her partner's **trade** is the household's anchor.
She admits she's **hoping more than knowing** about her new path.

steps.text: Start a part-time pharmacy technician course straight away
Pause the house purchase for a year
Keep saving at least 600 a month
Use AI tools to study for the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for thinking and 2034 for robots. So seven years for picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. I'd tell the younger ones at work to look into part-time courses now. I'd be fairly calm about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think it gives me time to train and still buy a house. But I'd still lose this job eventually. I'd be 34 when the robots come, which is a good age to change, but I'd rather already have changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year, a smaller one, and keep working. I'd start the pharmacy technician course in a year or two, once I saw others doing it. I'd keep a good chunk of savings separate from the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. Like knowing you've got a driving test in a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the house now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Jonah's trade looks solid for longer, and seven years of payments is a good start. If we wait for everything to be certain, we'll never buy. My mum always says that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the course sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the checking cameras arrive at our place. That's my sign. Once the computer is checking the tablets, I know the clock's ticking.

Start the **pharmacy technician** course in a year or two.

fieldNote: She has a clear **trigger**: checking cameras arriving at her workplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far off, let's be sensible and not panic. I'd say the government has time to get the training sorted. I'd probably not talk about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think that's fine for me. House bought, maybe a baby, and I'd have years to move into pharmacy work. My job's safe for a good while, but I'd still keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the next year or two and keep working. I'd do the cold room training for the extra pay. Pharmacy technician course maybe in three or four years, once I've seen how it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a bit. It's on the horizon but not on my doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Does the timing change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. In the two-year one I'd wait. With ten years I'd go ahead, because I'd have time to retrain after maternity leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kid to learn something with their hands and their head, both. That's what Jonah's doing, and he seems safest of anyone I know.

I'd say the government has **time** to sort out training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not because we'd be broke, we wouldn't, but because I'd have to decide everything at once: the house, the course, a baby. What would help is free part-time courses for people in work, and a clear warning from employers about which jobs are going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. A lot of what I'd do depends on my boyfriend's job, not mine, and most people don't decide on their own.

headlineQuote: A lot of what I'd do depends on my boyfriend's job, not mine, and most people don't decide on their own.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old picker** at a pharmacy supply warehouse, careful rather than fast.
She lives with Jonah, an **apprentice electrician**, and they're saving for a **house**.
She sees the **checking** part of her job going first, then picking after robots arrive.
Her plan is **pharmacy technician** training, and timing decides the house and a baby.
She is pragmatic and calm in public, and anxious in private when AGI comes fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing the house, the course and a baby to be decided at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Free part-time courses** for people in work.
Clear **warnings** from employers about which jobs are going.
